Subject: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling — follow-up from discovery call

Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Wanted to recap the key SLO and scaling points we discussed and call out the open questions so we can keep momentum on the POC & pricing discussion.

Recap (from the call)
- Target 95th percentile latency: <= 500ms for streaming chat responses (token-by-token streaming).
- Sustained throughput: ~120 reqs/min average during business hours, with spikes up to 800 reqs/min during batch runs.
- Concurrency: up to 60 concurrent live sessions.
- Burst requirements: ability to absorb 2-3x sustained traffic for short windows (5-15 minutes) with degradation strategy (graceful tail-latency vs. reject).
- Warm pool preference: you prefer a warm pool for sub-10s scale-up rather than cold cold-starts.

Open/Action items we promised to follow up on:
1) Concrete scale-up times with different warm-pool sizes and instance types (Dev to provide numbers).
2) Documented queueing behavior — at what point do we start buffering vs. shedding?
3) Streaming integration details (how streaming tokens are billed and how we preserve KV-cache across bursts).
4) Draft SLA language and example fallback policy (attached SLA draft).

Next steps
- Dev will send a short technical note with measured scale-up times and recommended warm-pool sizing by Fri (07/10).
- I’ll attach a draft SLA + mutual action plan for your procurement team to review (attached).
- If useful, let’s schedule a 45-min SRE deep-dive next week with your infra team + our SREs.

Hi Marissa —

Thanks for the clear notes. A couple of clarifying items from our side before the SRE deep-dive:

- For the 95p <= 500ms target: that’s for end-to-end streaming responses (we start the audio play-out as tokens arrive). If the system needs to buffer more than 200ms at the front-end, the UX team flags it. Can your warm pool guarantees cover sub-200ms median tail during spikes?

- For bursts: our busiest day last quarter peaked at ~1,200 reqs/min for 7 minutes during a promotional event. We need guidance on what size warm pool would give us <10s scale-up to handle that spike without significant request queuing.

- Also important: when you say "graceful tail-latency vs. reject" can you share examples of policies you typically recommend? E.g., prefer token-level slowing down, partial responses, or hard rejects?

We’re happy to do the SRE call next Tue 07/14 if that works for your team.

—Alex

Hi Alex / Priya —

Quick technical note answering your core questions. Short version up top, details below.

Short answers
- Warm-pool sizing: To cover a 1,200 req/min 7-min spike with <10s scale-up for typical LLM generate workloads (avg request ~120 tokens, streaming), we recommend a warm pool equivalent to ~30% of peak steady-state capacity. For your numbers that equates to ~250 warm slots (we can map to instance counts in the follow-up spreadsheet).
- Scale-up times: With warm pools already healthy, observed scale-up to route traffic to warm instances is sub-6s (DNS/routing+container assignment); cold-start from zero can be 45-120s depending on instance type and model warm-up (KV cache priming).
- Queueing vs shedding: We provide configurable policies: (1) queue up to configurable per-route backlog (recommended small: 30-60s per-request), (2) token-level backpressure for streaming — we can slow token emission rate to preserve 95p latency for in-flight sessions, (3) reject with HTTP 429 and detailed Retry-After when backlog exceeds safety threshold.

Details / assumptions
- The <6s number assumes: warm pool instances have model loaded with KV cache primed for typical prompt prefixes (we pre-warm with synthetic traffic every X mins). If you prefer absolute sub-2s tail, we’ll need more warm slots or a prioritized warm subset for VIP traffic.
- Billing & billing semantics during bursts: streaming tokens are billed by token generated; warm-pool idle allocation will be billed under reserved/dedicated capacity pricing if you choose dedicated. We can provide a cost projection for different warm pool sizes.
- Fallback examples: we commonly implement a three-tier fallback: (A) priority routing to lower-latency quantized variants for non-critical sessions; (B) temporary token-rate limiting (reduce tokens/sec); (C) hard rejects for unauthenticated or low-priority traffic.

I’ll attach a small spreadsheet mapping warm-slot counts to instance types and observed scale-up times. Happy to walk through on Tue 07/14 SRE call — propose 08:30 PT?

Thanks —
